summary: At 85 people per square mile spread across more than 3,300 square miles, San Luis Obispo County has roughly the population density of a national forest with a college town dropped in the middle — and that contrast defines daily life here. The county stretches from the dramatic Big Sur–adjacent coastline near San Simeon down through the volcanic morros (a chain of ancient peaked hills running from Morro Bay inland) to the rolling ranch and wine-grape land around Paso Robles, meaning the terrain shifts from coastal bluffs to oak-studded valleys within a thirty-minute drive. Cal Poly anchors the city of San Luis Obispo as both a major employer and an economic engine, alongside a healthcare sector centered on regional hospitals and a surprisingly robust wine industry — Paso Robles alone has over 200 wineries. That employment mix matters because the median household income of $93,398 faces a median home price of $777,200, an 8.3-to-1 ratio that puts ownership out of comfortable reach for a household earning the local median, while median rent at $1,899 consumes roughly 24% of that gross income — manageable but tight. The climate is genuinely unusual: an average daily high of 72°F year-round with nearly ten hours of sunshine per day, and summer nights that cool to the low 50s thanks to marine-layer influence. The county's defining tension is that its beauty and moderate weather have priced its economy beyond what most of its own jobs comfortably support.
